content.intro: In this lesson, you will study heuristic Search and Optimization within Traditional AI, Logic, Search, and Reasoning. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Traditional AI represents states, facts, goals, and actions explicitly. A search or rule-based method is only as useful as its representation and assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: A heuristic estimates how promising a state is. In A* search, the relationship between path cost and the heuristic affects whether an optimal solution is guaranteed, so admissibility and consistency assumptions matter.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Heuristic functions
items.text: A heuristic estimates which option is promising without necessarily calculating the exact answer. Evaluate whether that estimate is informative and whether it preserves any desired guarantees.

items.title: Greedy best-first search
items.text: Greedy best-first search is one of the concepts used to reason about heuristic search and optimization. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: A* search
items.text: A* orders paths using the known cost so far plus a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. Optimality depends on assumptions about the heuristic and path costs.

content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what heuristic search and optimization takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Traditional AI represents states, facts, goals, and actions explicitly. A search or rule-based method is only as useful as its representation and assumptions.

content_blocks.code:
inputs = [0.5, 1.0]
weights = [2.0, -1.0]
bias = 0.25
score = sum(x * w for x, w in zip(inputs, weights)) + bias
relu = max(0.0, score)
print("score:", round(score, 2))
print("relu:", round(relu, 2))
